tagline: The second volume of Luke's two-part work: how the risen Jesus, by his Spirit, carried the good news from a room in Jerusalem to the capital of the Roman world.
overview:
Acts picks up where the Gospel of Luke leaves off. The risen Jesus spends forty days with his apostles, tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into heaven. At the Jewish festival of Pentecost the Spirit comes, Peter preaches, and about three thousand people are baptized. From there the book follows the witness outward. The first community in Jerusalem shares its goods and faces arrest and threats; Stephen becomes the first martyr; persecution scatters believers into Judea and Samaria; Philip baptizes an Ethiopian official; and Saul of Tarsus, the church's fiercest opponent, meets the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. Peter is sent to the house of a Roman centurion named Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles (people who are not Jewish) just as it had on Jews.

The second half belongs largely to Saul, now called Paul. He and his companions travel through Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece, planting communities in cities like Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus. A council in Jerusalem (chapter 15) settles that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole law of Moses to belong to God's people. Paul is arrested in Jerusalem, defends himself before Jewish councils, Roman governors, and a Jewish king, appeals to Caesar, survives a shipwreck, and arrives in Rome. The book closes with him under house arrest for two years, welcoming everyone who comes and proclaiming the kingdom of God without hindrance.

Acts matters because it is the only narrative we have of the church's first three decades. Without it, Paul's letters would float without a setting, and the step from a Jewish teacher executed in Judea to communities of Jews and Gentiles meeting across the empire would be almost unexplained. It is also a theological book: it insists that the church's growth is the work of the risen Christ and his Spirit, not of clever strategy, and that the gospel crosses every boundary of language, race, and class.
author:
Like the Gospels, Acts is formally anonymous, but it is plainly the second half of a work that begins with the Gospel of Luke. Both are addressed to the same man, Theophilus (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1), and Acts opens by referring back to a first book about all that Jesus began to do and to teach. The style, vocabulary, and concerns of the two books match closely, and most scholars of every persuasion treat them as a single two-volume work, often called Luke-Acts.

From the late second century, church writers, among them Irenaeus of Lyon, name the author as Luke, a companion of Paul whom Paul's letters call a physician and fellow worker (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). The strongest internal evidence is the so-called we passages, stretches of the narrative where the story shifts from they to we (16:10-17; 20:5-15; 21:1-18; 27:1-28:16), which read most naturally as the writer's own presence on those voyages. Many scholars accept Luke as the author on this basis. Others think the we passages come from a travel source the author used, or are a literary device, and they point to differences between Acts and Paul's own letters as reasons to doubt that a close companion wrote it. The traditional view remains widely held and has strong support.
date:
Acts ends with Paul in Rome awaiting trial, about AD 60 to 62, and there are two main positions on when it was written. The first dates it to the early 60s, soon after that point. Its defenders note that the book never mentions Paul's death, the persecution under Nero in AD 64, the martyrdom of James the Lord's brother in AD 62, or the destruction of the temple in AD 70, all events it would have had reason to report, and they read the open ending as simply where events stood when Luke wrote.

The second, held by many modern scholars, dates it to the 70s or 80s. Its defenders argue that Luke's Gospel draws on Mark, often dated to the late 60s, that Luke 21:20 (armies surrounding Jerusalem) reflects knowledge of the Roman siege, and that the open ending is a deliberate literary choice: Luke's point is that the gospel reached Rome, not what became of Paul. A smaller group of scholars, such as Richard Pervo, argue for the early second century. The book's meaning does not depend on settling the question, but the earlier date would make Acts nearly contemporary with the events of its last chapters.
setting:
Acts covers roughly three decades, from the resurrection and Pentecost (about AD 30 or 33) to Paul's house arrest in Rome (about AD 60 to 62). The whole Mediterranean world was under Roman rule. Emperors from Tiberius to Nero reigned in Rome, while Judea was governed by Roman prefects and procurators, briefly by the Jewish king Herod Agrippa I (AD 41 to 44, whose death Acts 12 describes), and then by procurators again, including Felix and Festus, before whom Paul stood trial.

Jews lived not only in Judea but in communities across the empire (the Diaspora, or dispersion), with synagogues in most cities of any size. Around those synagogues gathered Gentiles who admired Israel's God without fully converting, often called God-fearers, and they are among the first Gentiles to believe in Acts. Greek was the common language of the eastern empire, Roman roads and sea lanes made travel possible, and Roman citizenship, which Paul held, carried legal protections that matter at several points in the story. The book moves through the religious world of the empire as well: the Jerusalem temple and its priestly leadership, the Pharisees and Sadducees, local cults like that of Artemis at Ephesus, magicians, philosophers at Athens, and the imperial courts.
purpose:
Luke tells Theophilus at the start of his Gospel that he writes so that his reader may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (Luke 1:4), and Acts continues that aim. It shows that the church's message rests on public events and on witnesses, and it explains how a movement that began among Jews came to include Gentiles without requiring them to become Jews. It defends the legitimacy of that inclusion as the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures and the plain work of God, not a betrayal of Israel.

Acts also answers questions a Roman reader might ask. Again and again Roman officials find no crime in Paul or the believers, which suggests that the movement is not a political threat to Rome. And it offers the church a model: a people who pray, share their goods, bear witness under pressure, settle disputes openly, and keep crossing boundaries at the Spirit's leading. Scholars debate how much weight each of these aims carries, but all of them are visible in the text.
story: Acts is the hinge between the Gospels and the letters. The Gospels end with Jesus risen and the command to make disciples of all nations; Acts shows that command being carried out, and it gives the setting for most of Paul's letters, which were written during the travels it describes. It also looks back across the whole Old Testament. God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and Isaiah spoke of Israel as a light to the nations. Acts presents the church as the place where those promises begin to be fulfilled. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost answers Joel's prophecy, and the confusion of languages at Babel is met by a gift in which many languages declare the works of God. The book ends not with a conclusion but with the gospel spreading, which leaves room for the rest of church history and for the final hope of Christ's return that the angels announce in chapter 1.
christ: Acts is sometimes called the Acts of the Apostles, but its first verse suggests a better title. Luke says his first book was about all that Jesus began to do and to teach, which implies that Acts is about what Jesus continues to do, now from heaven, through his Spirit and his people. The risen Christ appears, speaks, and acts throughout: he pours out the Spirit (2:33), stands at God's right hand as Stephen dies (7:56), confronts Saul on the Damascus road (9:5), and speaks to Paul in visions (18:9; 23:11). The apostles' preaching centers on his death, his resurrection as the vindication of God, his exaltation as Lord and Christ, and the forgiveness of sins offered in his name. Acts is the church's earliest narrative account of the conviction that Jesus is alive and reigning, and that his reign is advancing through witness rather than force.
reading:
Acts is historical narrative written by an ancient historian, and it follows the conventions of ancient history writing: speeches, summaries, selected episodes, and a clear theological point of view. Read it for its large movement, from Jerusalem outward, and notice the summary statements that mark stages of growth (for example 6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20).

The most common misreading treats every event in Acts as a rule for every church. Acts describes a unique period, the founding of the church, and some of what happens (the sound of wind at Pentecost, the lot cast for Matthias) is not presented as repeatable. At the same time the book clearly intends to shape its readers. Christians differ on how much of its pattern is normative, especially on the order of faith, baptism, and receiving the Spirit, and on whether speaking in tongues is a regular sign of the Spirit's coming. A careful reader asks of each episode what Luke himself signals is typical and what is exceptional, and reads Acts alongside the teaching of the letters.

The question of historical reliability has been debated for two centuries. In the nineteenth century the Tübingen school, led by F. C. Baur, argued that Acts smooths over real conflict between Peter and Paul, and some scholars still point to tensions between Acts and Paul's letters, for example in the number and purpose of Paul's visits to Jerusalem. Others, from William Ramsay to Colin Hemer in The Book of Acts in the Setting of Hellenistic History (1989), have stressed how often Luke gets local details right. An inscription from Delphi dates Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia to about AD 51 to 52, matching Acts 18:12; Luke correctly calls Sergius Paulus the proconsul of Cyprus (13:7); and he uses the unusual title politarchs for the city officials of Thessalonica (17:6), a title confirmed by inscriptions from that city. Both sides agree that Luke shaped his material; they differ on how freely.

structure.title: Waiting and Pentecost
structure.summary: The risen Jesus commissions his apostles and ascends. Matthias replaces Judas, and the Spirit comes at Pentecost, followed by Peter's sermon and the birth of the Jerusalem church.

structure.title: Witness in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Healing, preaching, arrest, and growth in the city. The church shares its goods, faces discipline and internal tension, and appoints seven to serve. Stephen's speech and death close the Jerusalem section.

structure.title: Judea, Samaria, and the door to the nations
structure.summary: Persecution scatters the church. Philip preaches in Samaria and to an Ethiopian, Saul is converted, Peter is sent to Cornelius, a mixed church forms at Antioch, and Herod Agrippa I opposes the apostles and dies.

structure.title: The first mission and the Jerusalem council
structure.summary: Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul through Cyprus and southern Asia Minor. The church in Jerusalem decides that Gentile believers need not be circumcised.

structure.title: Paul's missions around the Aegean
structure.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece and spends about three years in Ephesus, planting churches, facing riots, and finally setting his face toward Jerusalem.

structure.title: Paul on trial and the road to Rome
structure.summary: Paul is arrested in the temple, defends himself before crowds, councils, governors, and King Agrippa II, appeals to Caesar, survives a shipwreck, and preaches in Rome under house arrest.

themes.title: The Holy Spirit
themes.body: The Spirit is the driving force of Acts. Jesus promises the Spirit's power for witness (1:8), the Spirit comes at Pentecost, fills believers for bold speech, guides decisions, sets apart missionaries, and falls on Samaritans and Gentiles in ways that force the church to recognize them as full members. Luke uses several expressions for the Spirit's work (baptized with, filled with, poured out, received), and Christian traditions read these differently, but all agree that in Acts the church lives and moves by the Spirit rather than by its own resources.

themes.title: Witness
themes.body: The key word of the book's program is witness (1:8). The apostles are first of all witnesses of the resurrection, people who saw the risen Jesus and testify to it. Others then bear witness to what they have come to believe, often before hostile courts. The Greek word for witness later came to mean martyr, and in Acts the two ideas already touch: Stephen's witness costs him his life.

themes.title: The gospel crosses boundaries
themes.body: Acts traces the good news across line after line: from Jews in Jerusalem to Greek-speaking Jews, to Samaritans, to a eunuch from Ethiopia, to a Roman centurion, to pagans in Lystra and philosophers in Athens. Each crossing is contested, and the church often has to be pushed by God to accept it. The Jerusalem council in chapter 15 settles the central question: Gentiles are saved by grace through faith, as Jews are, without first becoming Jews.

themes.title: Continuity with Israel
themes.body: Acts insists that faith in Jesus fulfills Israel's hope rather than replacing it. The first believers are Jews who worship in the temple; the apostles preach from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; and Paul, even on trial, says he stands accused because of the hope of Israel. The book is honest that many of Paul's fellow Jews rejected his message, and it ends with that tension unresolved, but it never presents the church as a new religion cut loose from Israel's God.

themes.title: Suffering and the sovereignty of God
themes.body: Almost every advance in Acts comes through opposition: arrests, beatings, stonings, riots, and a shipwreck. Luke presents none of this as defeat. Persecution scatters the church and so spreads the word; Paul's imprisonment carries him to Rome at the empire's expense. God's purpose stands behind events without making the suffering less real.

keyChapters.why: The risen Jesus gives the program of the book (1:8) and ascends, with the promise that he will return.
The Spirit comes at Pentecost, and Peter's sermon sets out the first public proclamation of the risen Christ.
Stephen's long speech retells Israel's history and his death marks the end of the Jerusalem period and introduces Saul.
Saul, the persecutor, meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.
Peter's visit to Cornelius opens the door to the Gentiles, with the Spirit falling on them as on the first believers.
The Jerusalem council decides that Gentile believers are saved by grace without circumcision, a turning point for the whole church.
Paul's speech in Athens shows how the gospel addresses a pagan audience with no knowledge of Israel's Scriptures.
Paul reaches Rome, and the book ends with the kingdom proclaimed boldly and without hindrance at the empire's heart.

parts.body:
Acts is the fifth book of the New Testament, right after the four Gospels. It has 28 chapters. It is the second half of a two-part work. The same writer wrote the Gospel of Luke first, and both books are written to a man called Theophilus.

Luke's Gospel told the story of Jesus. Acts tells what happened next. It opens with the risen Jesus, who tells his followers to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit and is then taken up into heaven. At the Jewish feast of Pentecost the Spirit comes, Peter preaches to the crowds, and about three thousand people are baptized.

From there the story moves outward, step by step. The first believers in Jerusalem share their goods and face arrest. Stephen is stoned to death. The believers scatter into the country around. Saul, who had hunted them, meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus. Peter visits the house of a Roman army officer, and people who are not Jews (the Bible calls them Gentiles) receive the Spirit too. The second half follows Saul, now called Paul, across what is now Turkey and Greece, and at last to Rome as a prisoner.

The book ends with Paul under guard in Rome, still teaching: “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ” (28:31). It does not say what happened to him next. The story is left open, as if more were still to be written.

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how we know
parts.body:
Like the Gospels, Acts does not name its writer. But it plainly comes from the same hand as the Gospel of Luke. Both are written to Theophilus, and Acts begins, “In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach” (1:1). The first book is Luke's Gospel. The style and the favourite words of the two books match closely, and nearly all scholars treat them as one work in two volumes.

The early church named the writer as Luke. Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul (modern France), writing around AD 180, said that Luke was Paul's companion and that he set down in a book the gospel Paul preached. An early list of the Bible's books, called the Muratorian fragment and usually dated to the late second century, says that Luke wrote ‘the acts of all the apostles’ in one book for Theophilus, telling the things that happened while he was there. Paul's letters name a Luke among his fellow workers: “Luke, the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14; also Philemon 24 and 2 Timothy 4:11).

The strongest clue is inside the book itself. In a few stretches the story suddenly says ‘we’ instead of ‘they’: “we got ready to leave for Macedonia” (16:10). These are called the ‘we’ passages (16:10-17; 20:5 to 21:18; 27:1 to 28:16). Irenaeus already read them as a sign that the writer travelled with Paul.

Scholars read the ‘we’ passages in more than one way. Many take them the plain way: the writer was there. Others think the writer used a travel diary kept by someone who was there. A few have argued that ‘we’ was simply a way of telling sea voyages in the writing of the time, and others dispute that such a custom existed. Some scholars also doubt that a close friend of Paul wrote Acts, because they see differences between Acts and Paul's own letters (the part ‘Acts and Paul's letters’ below sets them out). Others answer that two friends can tell the same events in different ways for different purposes. The traditional view, that Luke the companion of Paul wrote it, is still widely held.

Luke and Acts were written as one story in two parts. Luke's Gospel ends with the risen Jesus telling his disciples to “remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49), and then being carried up into heaven. Acts begins with the same scene, told again at more length.

The two books mirror each other. In the first, the Spirit comes on Jesus at his baptism, and he begins his work with a sermon (Luke 3 and 4). In the second, the Spirit comes on the disciples at Pentecost, and Peter begins with a sermon (Acts 2). Jesus heals a man who cannot walk (Luke 5:17-26); so do Peter (Acts 3) and Paul (Acts 14:8-10). Jesus prays for the men who kill him (Luke 23:34); so does Stephen (Acts 7:60). Jesus goes up to Jerusalem knowing what waits for him there; so does Paul, who says he is “ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:13).

The point is in the first verse. The Gospel told what Jesus “began to do and to teach” (1:1). Acts tells what he goes on doing, now from heaven, by his Spirit, through his people. That is why some readers say the book could as well be called the Acts of the risen Jesus, or the Acts of the Holy Spirit, as the Acts of the Apostles. Most of the twelve apostles hardly appear after the first chapter. The book is mostly about Peter, and then about Paul.

Acts gives no date. Its last scene is Paul in Rome, under guard for “two full years” (28:30), which most date to about AD 60 to 62. So Acts was finished after that. How long after is debated, and there are three main views.

The early 60s. Some scholars date Acts soon after its last scene. Their main reason is what the book leaves out. Paul is the hero of the second half, yet the book never says how his trial ended or that he died. It does not mention the great fire of Rome in July 64, after which the emperor Nero blamed the Christians and many were put to death, as the Roman historian Tacitus tells. It does not mention that James, the brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church in Acts, was stoned in Jerusalem around AD 62, which the Jewish historian Josephus reports. It does not mention the fall of Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70. On this view, Luke stopped where he stopped because events had reached his own day.

The 70s or 80s. Many modern scholars, probably most, date Acts here, with Luke's Gospel a little before it. They think Luke used Mark's Gospel, which is often dated to the late 60s, and that Luke's Gospel shows knowledge of how the Roman siege of Jerusalem went (Luke 19:43; 21:20). They read the open ending as a choice. The story was heading for Rome all along, and its last words show the message preached there without hindrance. The goal was reached, so the book was done.

Early in the second century. A smaller group dates Acts later still. Richard Pervo, in Dating Acts (2006), argued for about AD 115, partly because he thought Acts used a collection of Paul's letters and the writings of Josephus. Most scholars have not followed him.

Each view has careful defenders, and these notes do not settle the question. Nothing in the faith hangs on the year.

parts.h: What kind of book it is
parts.body:
Acts is a history book, written the way history was written in the ancient world. That is different from a modern history in some ways and the same in others.

Like other ancient histories, it chooses. It covers about thirty years in 28 chapters and leaves out far more than it tells. Most of the apostles drop out of sight. We hear nothing of the first believers in Egypt or in the lands to the east. Luke picks the stories that show how the message went from Jerusalem to Rome.

It marks its stages with short summaries: “So the word of God continued to spread” (6:7; compare 9:31, 12:24, 16:5 and 19:20). They work like the end of a chapter in a modern book.

And it is full of speeches. A large part of the book is people speaking: Peter at Pentecost, Stephen before the council, Paul in a synagogue, in Athens and before a king. That raises a fair question. Did Luke have a record of every word? Most of the speeches take only a few minutes to read aloud, and the real ones were surely longer.

Ancient historians knew this question. The Greek historian Thucydides, writing in the 400s BC, said of the speeches in his history that exact words were hard to remember, so he kept as close as he could to the general sense of what was really said, and gave the speakers what the moment called for. Not every later historian was as careful, and some were criticised for making speeches up.

Readers understand the speeches of Acts in more than one way. Many think they are faithful summaries: the general sense of what was said, in Luke's words. They point out that the speeches differ from one another in ways that suit their speakers and settings, and that some ways of speaking about Jesus in Peter's early sermons, such as God's ‘servant’ (3:13), seem to come from the church's earliest days. Other scholars think Luke wrote the speeches himself, as many ancient historians did, to say what he believed each moment meant, so that they tell us more about Luke than about Peter or Paul. Many hold a view somewhere between. All agree that the speeches are short, that Luke shaped them, and that they carry much of the book's teaching.

Acts gives its own outline near the start. Jesus tells his followers, “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8).

The book follows that order. Chapters 1 to 7 stay in Jerusalem. Chapters 8 to 12 move into Judea, the country around Jerusalem, and Samaria, the region to the north whose people most Jews kept apart from, and on to the coast and to Damascus. In chapter 10 the message reaches a Roman officer and his household. From chapter 13 it goes out into the wider world: Cyprus, the cities of what is now Turkey, then Greece, and at last Rome.

‘The ends of the earth’ is a phrase from Israel's prophets. In Isaiah, God says to his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Paul and Barnabas quote those words when they turn to the Gentiles (13:47).

Rome was not the end of the earth, and Luke knew it. But it was the centre of the world his readers knew. When the message is preached openly there, the book stops. The rest of the road is left to those who come after.

The outline at the top of this page draws Acts in six parts: waiting and Pentecost (1 and 2); witness in Jerusalem (3 to 7); Judea, Samaria and the door to the nations (8 to 12); the first mission and the council in Jerusalem (13:1 to 15:35); Paul's travels around the Aegean Sea (15:36 to 21:16); and Paul on trial and the road to Rome (21:17 to 28:31).

Seen from further back, the book has two halves. Peter leads the first half and Paul the second. Luke seems to have shaped them to match. Both heal a man lame from birth (3:1-10; 14:8-10). Both see prison doors opened in the night (12:6-11; 16:25-26). Both are taken for more than men and refuse it (10:25-26; 14:11-15). Both raise a dead person to life (9:36-41; 20:9-12). The same Spirit works through both, and the message they preach is the same.

At the hinge stands chapter 15. The church meets in Jerusalem to decide whether Gentiles who believe in Jesus must first become Jews. Peter speaks for the last time in the book, and after that the story belongs to Paul.

The Holy Spirit. The Spirit drives the story. Jesus promises power when the Spirit comes (1:8), and the Spirit gives the believers courage to speak, guides their choices, sends out Paul and Barnabas, and comes on Samaritans and Gentiles in ways that push the church to accept them.

Witness. A witness tells what he has seen. The apostles are first of all people who saw Jesus alive after his death (1:22). The Greek word for witness, martus, later came to mean martyr, someone who dies for the faith. In Acts the two meanings already touch: Stephen's witness costs him his life.

The good news crosses lines. The message goes from Jews in Jerusalem to Greek-speaking Jews, to Samaritans, to an official from Ethiopia, to a Roman officer, to farmers in Lystra and thinkers in Athens. Each crossing is argued over, and often God has to push the church across it.

God's promises to Israel kept. The first believers are Jews who pray in the temple. The apostles preach from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms. Paul, on trial, says he is bound “because of the hope of Israel” (28:20). Acts never treats the church as a new religion cut loose from Israel's God.

Suffering that does not stop the word. Almost every step forward comes through trouble: arrests, beatings, riots, a shipwreck. Persecution scatters the believers and so spreads the message. Paul's chains carry him to Rome. Luke does not make the suffering small, and he does not treat it as defeat.

Acts is soaked in Israel's Scriptures. The first sermons are built from them. At Pentecost Peter explains what is happening by the prophet Joel: “In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (2:17, from Joel 2:28). He then argues from Psalm 16, where David says to God, “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (2:27), and from Psalm 110, where the Lord says to the king, “Sit at My right hand” (2:34). In chapter 4 the believers pray Psalm 2 and Peter quotes Psalm 118: “the stone you builders rejected” (4:11).

Stephen's long speech in chapter 7 retells Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon. When the church decides about the Gentiles in chapter 15, James quotes the prophet Amos: God will rebuild “the fallen tent of David” so that all the nations may seek the Lord (15:16-17, from Amos 9:11-12). And the book ends with Paul quoting Isaiah 6 to the Jewish leaders in Rome (28:26-27).

Most of these quotations follow the Septuagint, the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible that Greek-speaking Jews read, so their wording sometimes differs from the Hebrew behind our Old Testaments. The notes on each chapter point this out where it matters.

The claim running under all of it is simple. What has happened in Jesus is not a new story but the next chapter of Israel's story, the one the prophets were waiting for.

parts.h: Acts and the history of its day
parts.body:
Acts names rulers, cities and officials, and that makes it possible to check. Some of its details can be matched with other ancient sources.

Herod Agrippa I. Acts 12 tells how King Herod, known to historians as Herod Agrippa I, killed James the brother of John, and later died suddenly at Caesarea after the crowd hailed his voice as “the voice of a god” (12:22). The Jewish historian Josephus tells the same death: at Caesarea, during games held for the emperor, the people hailed Agrippa as a god, he did not rebuke them, and he was seized with pain in his belly and died five days later. Josephus places it in the seventh year of the emperor Claudius, AD 44. The two accounts differ in detail, but they tell the same event.

The famine. A prophet in Acts foretells a great famine, and Luke adds, “This happened under Claudius” (11:28). Josephus tells of a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s, under the governors Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, when Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain in Egypt and figs in Cyprus for the people of Jerusalem. Most think this is the famine Acts means, though its exact years are uncertain.

Claudius and the Jews of Rome. In Corinth, Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, who had come from Italy “because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome” (18:2). The Roman writer Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they kept making disturbances at the prompting of ‘Chrestus’. Most scholars think this is a garbled form of ‘Christus’, and that the trouble was over Jesus; some think Chrestus was a local troublemaker. The year usually given, AD 49, comes from a much later writer, Orosius, and is disputed.

Gallio. Acts says Paul was brought before Gallio “while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia” (18:12). A proconsul was the governor of a Roman province. A letter of Claudius, carved in stone at Delphi in Greece, names Gallio and allows his year of office to be fixed, most think in AD 51 to 52, some say 50 to 51. This is the surest fixed date in Paul's life, and the other dates of his travels are counted from it.

City officials. In Thessalonica, Luke calls the city's rulers by a rare title, politarchs, translated ‘city officials’ (17:6). Inscriptions using that title have been found there; the best known came from an old arch over the main Roman road and is now in the British Museum.

What this shows is debated. Some scholars gather many such details and argue that Luke was a careful historian who can be trusted where he cannot be checked. Others answer that getting local details right does not prove every story, and that Luke shaped his material to teach, as all ancient historians did. Both sides agree that Luke knew the world he wrote about.

Paul wrote many of his letters during the years Acts describes, so the two can be read side by side. Often they fit well. Acts tells how Paul founded the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth, and his letters to those churches remember the same beginnings. But in some places readers see tensions, and it is fair to name them.

Paul's visits to Jerusalem. In Galatians, Paul is defending his right to preach, and he swears, “I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie” (Galatians 1:20). He says that after he met Jesus he went away to Arabia and back to Damascus. “Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days” (Galatians 1:18), and he saw no other apostle but James. Acts 9 says that “after many days” Paul went to Jerusalem and Barnabas brought him to the apostles (9:23-27), with no mention of Arabia.

Then Galatians says, “Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas” (Galatians 2:1), and that he met the leaders privately. Acts tells of two later visits by Paul and Barnabas: one to bring gifts in a famine (11:30), and one for the council of chapter 15. Which one is Galatians 2?

Readers answer in three ways. Many think Galatians 2 is the council of Acts 15, because both are about whether Gentiles must be circumcised. Others think it is the famine visit of Acts 11, because Paul went “in response to a revelation” (Galatians 2:2), as a prophet had foretold the famine, and the leaders asked him to “remember the poor” (Galatians 2:10); on this view Galatians was written before the council, which explains why Paul never mentions its decision. A third view sees Galatians 2 as a private meeting of its own.

Other tensions are noticed too. Galatians tells of a sharp quarrel between Paul and Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14) that Acts does not tell. And Paul warns the Galatians against being circumcised, yet in Acts he circumcises his helper Timothy (16:3).

Here too scholars differ. Some take these as signs that Acts was written later, by someone who did not know Paul closely or who smoothed over old quarrels to show a united church. Others think the two fit once their purposes are seen: Paul in Galatians is showing that his gospel did not come from the Jerusalem leaders, so he counts every contact; Luke is telling the church's story and leaves much out. They add that Galatians is about whether Gentiles must be circumcised to belong to God's people, while Timothy, whose mother was Jewish, was circumcised so that he could work among Jews. These notes set out the views and do not settle them.

Acts begins in Jerusalem among Jews. The apostles are Jews. The three thousand baptized at Pentecost are Jews and converts to Judaism, from all over the world. The first believers pray in the temple and keep the hours of prayer. “A great number of priests became obedient to the faith” (6:7). Years later, the leaders in Jerusalem tell Paul that “many thousands of Jews have believed” (21:20). Paul goes first to the synagogue in town after town, and he calls himself, on trial, “a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee” (23:6).

Acts also tells of conflict. In the early chapters Peter says to the crowds in Jerusalem that they put Jesus to death: “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (2:36). It matters who is speaking, and to whom. A Jew is speaking to his own people, in their own city, weeks after the event, about something done there. In the same breath he says Jesus was delivered up “by God's set plan and foreknowledge” (2:23), and soon after, “I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders” (3:17). And he offers them forgiveness, not condemnation: God sent his servant “first to you to bless you” (3:26). Three thousand of the hearers believe.

Later in the book, Luke often writes ‘the Jews’ for those in a city who opposed Paul (for example 9:23). He means the opponents in that place, not every Jew; in the same cities many Jews believed.

Over the centuries Christians misused verses like these to blame the whole Jewish people for Jesus' death, and called Jews ‘Christ-killers’. That reading fed contempt, expulsion and murder. It is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it, as on the pages for the four Gospels. Acts itself places all people inside the guilt: the first believers pray that “Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel” against Jesus (4:27). Jew and Gentile, ruler and crowd, together. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and many Protestant churches have said the same.

The book ends in Rome with Paul and the Jewish leaders there. “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe” (28:24). Paul tells them that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. Readers differ on what that ending means: a turn away from mission to the Jews, or a sad but open door, since Paul goes on welcoming “all who came to visit him” (28:30). Acts does not give a verdict on the Jewish people. It tells of a Jewish Messiah and his Jewish apostles, welcomed by many of their own and refused by others, as the prophets had been before them.

Acts is not a rulebook in which every event is a pattern for every church. It tells what happened at the church's founding, and some of what happened is plainly not meant to repeat. The sound of wind at Pentecost does not come again. Lots are cast once, to choose Matthias, and never again in the New Testament. No other believer is struck dead as Ananias and Sapphira are.

But Luke also clearly means the book to shape its readers. The first believers' devotion to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer (2:42) has been a pattern for churches ever since.

So the real question is which parts are meant to be normal, and Christians differ over it. Three places show the difference most. First, the Spirit. In Acts the Spirit sometimes comes at the moment of faith, sometimes after baptism (8:16), sometimes before it (10:44-48), and sometimes with speaking in tongues. Pentecostal Christians take some of these scenes as a pattern of a later filling with the Spirit; many others take them as unusual moments in a church crossing new lines. Second, baptism: who receives it, and how it relates to forgiveness (the notes on 2:38 set out the views). Third, shared goods: the believers of chapters 2 and 4 share what they own, freely and not by law (5:4), and churches differ on what, if anything, that asks of Christians now.

A careful reader asks of each scene what Luke himself signals is ordinary and what is a one-time turning point, and reads Acts alongside the teaching of the letters. Faithful churches land in different places on these questions, and these notes lay out the views without choosing between them.

Read it as one story. Acts takes a few hours to read aloud, and reading it in one or two sittings shows its movement better than anything else: from one room in Jerusalem to the capital of the empire.

Watch the summaries. Each time Luke says the word kept spreading (6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20), a stage of the story closes.

Watch who is speaking. The speeches carry the teaching. Ask what each speaker knows about his hearers, and how he begins where they are: with Joel for Jews at a feast, with the Creator and an altar ‘to an unknown god’ for thinkers in Athens (17:23).

Keep the letters near. When Acts reaches Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth or Ephesus, reading Paul's letter to that church shows the same story from the inside.

And notice who the book is really about. The apostles fail, argue and are afraid. The church is never perfect. But the risen Jesus keeps acting, and the word keeps going on.

hard.line: How did Judas die? Matthew says he hanged himself; Acts says he fell and burst open. The difference, faced honestly, and the ways readers answer it.
Tongues at Pentecost: known languages, heard by people from many lands. And how Christians differ on the gift of tongues today.
‘Whom you crucified’. Said by a Jew to his own people, with forgiveness offered. Why this verse may never be turned against the Jewish people.
‘Repent and be baptized’ for ‘the forgiveness of your sins’. How the churches read baptism, forgiveness and ‘your children’.
‘Everything in common’. What the first believers did, freely, and why it is not a program for any modern economy.
‘No other name’. What the text claims about Jesus, and where Christians differ about those who never heard.
Ananias and Sapphira. A hard story, not softened: what their sin was, and how readers have understood the judgment.
Gamaliel's Theudas, and the Theudas of Josephus who seems to come later. The problem stated honestly, and the answers given.
Stephen places Abraham's purchase at Shechem; Genesis puts it at Hebron. How readers account for the difference.
Believers in Samaria baptized, yet without the Spirit until the apostles came. One time, or a pattern?
Did Paul's companions hear the voice (9:7) or not understand it (22:9)? What the Greek allows.
The council's four rules for Gentile believers. Food laws, or something else? And do they still bind?
The salvation of God ‘sent to the Gentiles’. Does Acts end by closing the door to the Jews? Two readings.

words.line: Greek martus. One who tells what he has seen. The apostles are witnesses of the risen Jesus (1:8, 1:22); the word later came to mean martyr.
God's own Spirit, promised by Jesus and poured out at Pentecost (1:5, 2:4, 2:33). In Acts the Spirit gives courage and guides the church.
Greek for ‘fiftieth’. The Jewish Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when the Spirit came (2:1).
One who is sent. In Acts mostly the Twelve, who had been with Jesus and saw him risen (1:21-22); Paul and Barnabas are also called apostles (14:14).
Greek metanoeō, to change one's mind and turn one's life around (2:38, 3:19).
In the Bible a name stands for the person and his authority. Acts heals, baptizes and preaches ‘in the name of Jesus’ (3:6, 4:12).
Greek parrēsia, open and free speech without fear (4:13, 4:29). The last word of Acts describes Paul preaching ‘boldly’ (28:31).
An early name for the followers of Jesus and their way of life (9:2, 19:9, 24:14).
A name first given to the disciples at Antioch (11:26); in Acts it is used by outsiders (26:28).
People who are not Jews. Acts is in large part the story of how they came to share in Israel's promises (10:45, 15:7-11).
The council of leading priests, elders and teachers of the law in Jerusalem, led by the high priest (4:15, 5:21).
A Gentile who has fully joined the Jewish people; the BSB says ‘convert to Judaism’ (2:11, 6:5).
Greek ekklēsia, an assembly or gathering. The word Acts uses for the believers together (5:11, 8:1).

timeline.what: Pontius Pilate governs Judea. Peter reminds the crowd that Pilate had decided to release Jesus (3:13; 4:27).
The two dates most often proposed for Jesus' death and rising. Pentecost (2:1) comes seven weeks later.
The first believers in Jerusalem; Stephen's death; Saul meets the risen Jesus near Damascus (chapters 2 to 9).
Claudius is emperor. Acts names him for a famine (11:28) and for sending the Jews out of Rome (18:2).
Herod Agrippa I rules as king over Judea. He has James the brother of John put to death (12:1-2).
Agrippa dies suddenly at Caesarea, as Acts 12:20-23 and Josephus both tell, in the seventh year of Claudius.
A severe famine in Judea, according to Josephus. The church in Antioch sends help by Barnabas and Saul (11:28-30).
Claudius expels Jews from Rome. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Gallio is proconsul of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul stands before him in Corinth (18:12).
Nero is emperor. He is the ‘Caesar’ to whom Paul appeals (25:11).
Paul under guard in Rome for two years, where Acts ends (28:30).
James, the brother of Jesus and a leader in Jerusalem, is stoned, as Josephus reports. Acts does not tell it.
The great fire of Rome. Nero blames the Christians, and many are killed (Tacitus). Acts does not tell it.
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
When Acts was written: the early 60s on one view, the 70s or 80s on the view of many scholars. A few say about 115.
The Muratorian fragment, usually dated here, says Luke wrote the acts of all the apostles for Theophilus.
Irenaeus writes that Luke, Paul's companion, wrote down the gospel Paul preached, and reads the ‘we’ passages as Luke's.

map.name: Damascus
map.line: An old city in Syria. Saul asks for letters to its synagogues (9:2), meets the risen Jesus on the road to it, and is baptized there.

map.name: Sidon
map.line: A port city on the coast north of Galilee. With Tyre, it asks Herod Agrippa for peace because it depends on his land for food (12:20).

map.name: Tyre
map.line: The other great port of Phoenicia, south of Sidon. Its people come to Herod Agrippa at Caesarea to ask for peace (12:20).

map.name: Caesarea
map.line: A port city Herod the Great built on the coast, where the Roman governors lived. Cornelius, a Roman officer, lives here (10:1), and Herod Agrippa dies here (12:23).

map.name: Samaria
map.line: The region between Galilee and Judea, whose people most Jews kept apart from. Philip preaches the Christ in a city there (8:5).

map.name: Joppa
map.line: An old port, today's Jaffa. Peter raises Tabitha here, and on a rooftop here he sees the vision that sends him to Cornelius (9:36 to 10:16).

map.name: Lydda
map.line: A town inland from Joppa, today's Lod. Peter heals Aeneas here (9:32-35).

map.name: Jerusalem
map.line: Where the book begins. The Spirit comes here at Pentecost, the first believers meet in the temple courts, and Stephen is stoned outside the city (7:58).

map.name: Azotus
map.line: The old Philistine city of Ashdod, near the coast. Philip appears here after baptizing the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza (8:26-40).

teaching.mapNote: This map shows the land where Acts 1 to 12 happens. Gaza (8:26) lies just south of its edge. Paul's travels, from Antioch to Rome, need a wider map of the Mediterranean, which is still to come.
